title: Richness of Japanese culture in Northern Ireland celebrated
content:
Richness of Japanese culture in Northern Ireland celebrated
- Published
A day of vibrant music, song and dance has been held to celebrate the richness of Japanese culture in Northern Ireland.
The 30th anniversary of the Japan Society in Northern Ireland was marked with a family-friendly matsuri festival that featured performances, workshops, demonstrations and activities.
The Japanese Ambassador to the UK, and social media personality, Hiroshi Suzuki was in attendance and said he was excited to be there.
"For me this is extremely important – because there are a number of Japanese companies invested and operating in and around Belfast in Northern Ireland – and we have a mutually beneficial economic partnership," he said.
'Paddington is my partner'
Suzuki often carries around a Paddington Bear toy, and frequently posts pictures of it on social media, when he is travelling around the UK.
"Paddington is my partner, he helps me go around the UK – and thanks to Paddington I am a little bit popular on my X ( social media)," he said.
"My activities can be seen through Paddington, so I hope many people who can't be here today will get to see what kind of fantastic time we've had at Japan matsuri through my X, through the power of Paddington."
The event was held at W5 Belfast and featured storytelling, drama performances and sumo wrestling.
Sean Greer is the secretary of the Japan Society in Northern Ireland. He said the society was founded for people who are Japanese and live in Northern Ireland, but also for people from Northern Ireland who have lived in Japan:
"These days people are travelling to Japan more and more and becoming more aware of Japanese food and things like cherry blossoms. Japanese pop culture is big here in Northern Ireland as well."
Nicole Murray attended the event with her husband and said they wanted to meet new people at the festival:
"Belfast is becoming a really multi diverse city. For us it was just something we really wanted to check out – and we really enjoy the culture. So far, my favourite bit has been the Taiko drumming. "
'It is really interesting to see the heritage'
Junko McNeely is originally from Japan and attended with her son 15-year-old Joel. McNeely said the event showcased the connection between Japan and Northern Ireland.
"There are a variety of clubs associated with Japanese culture. The public can enjoy seeing what is available in Northern Ireland."
Joel said the event was important for him and others who have Japanese heritage.
"It's really interesting to see the heritage on my mum's side and get to know more, as growing up here – I don't get to experience as much of my Japanese side."

title: Philippine president pardons drug convict Mary Jane Veloso
content:
“I already signed her pardon,” Marcos told reporters.
Veloso returned to the Philippines in December 2024 following years of negotiations between Manila and Jakarta after spending nearly 15 years in prison in Indonesia.
Veloso, a mother of two and a former domestic helper, was arrested in Yogyakarta in 2010 after authorities found 2.6 kg (5.7 lb) of heroin concealed in a suitcase.
She said she was an unwitting drug mule, but she was convicted and sentenced to death in Indonesia.
Her case drew widespread attention in the Philippines, and prompted years of diplomatic efforts by Manila to secure clemency and eventually her transfer from Indonesia.
In 2024, Manila and Jakarta agreed to transfer Veloso back to Manila in a deal that included the Philippines respecting the court’s sentencing of Veloso and her status as a prisoner.
Indonesian authorities had said any decision on granting Veloso clemency after her transfer would be up to Marcos.

title: Sirijoje – pirmos moterys policininkės: tokiu būdu siekiama pelnyti Vakarų palaikymą
content:
Pirmoji Moterų policijos akademija Sirijoje išleido pirmąsias absolventes – 150 moterų papildys šalies teisėsaugos gretas. Taip nauja Sirijos valdžia bando atgaivinti karo išsekintas saugumo pajėgas ir pelnyti Vakarų palaikymą, nors tikrai lyčių lygybei pasiekti šaliai reikėtų daugybės reformų.
Vaikystės svajonės pildosi. 150 sirių švenčia – jos baigė naują Moterų policijos akademiją.
„Prisijungiau prie policijos pajėgų, nes tai buvo vaikystės svajonė ir troškau ją išpildyti. Kai tik prasidėjo atranka, skubėjau prisijungti“, – pasakoja Moterų policijos akademijos absolventė Mai Akladžne.
Intensyvus fizinis ir karinis pasirengimas truko šešis mėnesius. Moterys taip pat išklausė žmogaus teisių pagrindų kursą.
„Iš pradžių buvo sunku, tačiau nė karto nesigailėjau čia atėjusi. Per mokymus jautėmės laimingos, mokėmės drausmės ir teisės pagrindų. Tai buvo visapusiški mokymai“, – sako Moterų policijos akademijos absolventė Ala Kasem Vafa.
Basharo al Asado diktatūros metais moterys sudarė labai mažą policijos ir kariuomenės dalį, tačiau jų atvaizdai naudoti modernaus ir vakarietiško lyderio įvaizdžiui kurti.
Režimui sugriuvus, nauja Sirijos valdžia bando įveikti išbandymą – atkurti karo nualintos šalies saugumo sistemą. Naujoji moterų policijos akademija – vienas iš sprendimų.
„Įtraukti moteris į saugumo sektorių – būtina. O vėliau – ir į kitas profesines sritis“, – teigia Moterų policijos akademijos direktorė Huda Sardžavi.
Naujoji Sirijos valdžia žada paversti šalį demokratiškesne, plėsti diplomatinius ryšius ir gerinti sirų gyvenimo sąlygas. Tiesa, kol kas pažadai menkai įgyvendinti – moterų teisės šalyje suvaržytos, o valdžioje joms neatstovaujama.

title: Alcaldía de Chacao comenzó la fase 2 del plan de recuperación tras doble terremoto
content:
Gustavo Duque, alcalde de Chacao, anunció el comienzo de la segunda fase del plan de recuperación y acompañamiento a los vecinos afectados del sector, tras cumplirse tres meses del doble terremoto que afectó a Venezuela el 24 de junio de 2026.
El alcalde mencionó que la nueva fase, denominada “Reconstruyendo en equipo”, consta de cinco pasos y está enfocada principalmente en atender a los ciudadanos mayores de 55 años de edad que tienen la capacidad de costear la mano de obra para la reconstrucción de sus casas.
“Después de 3 meses de este doblete sísmico que nos cambió la vida a todos, quiero anunciarles que ¡Seguimos trabajando para que todos nuestros vecinos vuelvan a casa!”, afirmó Duque en una publicación que hizo en su cuenta de Instagram.
Duque resaltó que esta medida nace de la iniciativa de los propios vecinos, quienes indicaban que podían pagar la mano de obra si la alcaldía ofrecía los materiales, por lo que ese será el mecanismo de trabajo.
Detalles de la segunda fase de la recuperación de Chacao
El alcalde confirmó que los materiales para la reconstrucción de las viviendas serán otorgados por la alcaldía, pero la mano de obra será aportada por el vecino afectado.
Además, habrá tres controles para garantizar que los materiales entregados sean utilizados realmente en la reparación del apartamento. El primero será previo a la entrega, cuando los interesados deberán llenar un formulario de solicitud para la dotación de materiales.
Luego, durante toda la reparación, se mantendrá un acompañamiento para asegurar el buen uso de los insumos. Por último, se ejecutará un control posterior cuando la obra culmine.
La entrega y dotación de materiales se llevará a cabo progresivamente, a medida que avance la obra. Por su parte, se realizará la certificación de la obra y el cambio de etiqueta cuando esté culminada.
El plan contempla principalmente a adultos mayores de 55 años que tengan la capacidad económica. Sin embargo, también se contempla la integración de hogares que tengan niños en edad escolar o niños con condiciones especiales comprobadas a través del censo.
Los formularios de solicitud podrán llenarse mediante un portal web creado por la Alcaldía de Chacao y deberán ser completados por los cabezas de familia que hicieron el primer censo.
Duque explicó que la decisión responde a la situación de adultos mayores que, tras las afectaciones registradas en sus viviendas, no cuentan con los recursos necesarios para llevar a cabo las reparaciones por cuenta propia.
Primera fase de reparación en Chacao
Desde el 3 de agosto, la Alcaldía de Chacao inició un plan de recuperación de apartamentos y edificios afectados por los terremotos, con una primera etapa dirigida a vecinos mayores de 65 años cuyas viviendas presenten daños clasificados como amarillos o rojos, informó el alcalde Gustavo Duque.
El alcalde de Chacao recordó que la primera fase consistió en ejecutar un censo que incorporó a la mayoría de los condominios, donde se ubicaron las etiquetas verdes, amarillas y rojas, y se tuvo noción de cuántos apartamentos tenían afectaciones entre moderadas y severas.
Asimismo, indicó que un mes y medio después de los sismos se entregaron 11 edificios y casi 100 apartamentos que cuentan con condiciones de “dignidad para que los residentes puedan regresar a sus hogares”, reconstruidos y reparados.

title: What Kenyan law says about reporting child abuse
content:
What Kenyan law says about reporting child abuse
What you need to know:
- A teacher’s quick action after noticing signs of abuse helped trigger an intervention that rescued a 10-year-old girl and ultimately led to her father’s conviction.
- Kenyan law places a responsibility on anyone with reasonable cause to believe a child is at risk to report suspected abuse and seek protection.
On May 26, 2019, a woman left for church, leaving her 10-year-old niece and two daughters at home with her brother. The niece was her brother’s daughter. When the woman returned that evening, she found the children at home.
The following morning, she prepared the children and escorted them to school. But that evening, her niece did not return home. When she made inquiries, she learnt that the girl had left school earlier than usual. She later discovered that the child had been taken to a children’s home.
Why?
When the girl arrived at school that morning, her teacher noticed that she appeared to be in pain and smelled of faeces. Concerned, the teacher referred her to another teacher, who reported the matter to the headteacher.
A community health volunteer was subsequently informed that the girl had allegedly been defiled. She immediately went to the school and took the child to Kilimani police station. They were referred to Capitol Hill police station, where a report was filed. Statements were recorded and the child was issued with a P3 form, which was completed at Nairobi Women’s Hospital, where she was examined.
The examination established that the girl had been sexually abused by her father, who had penetrated her anus. The chain of intervention, from the teacher who noticed that something was wrong, to the community health volunteer, police and medical personnel, helped rescue the child and secure her safety.
The girl’s father was eventually arrested and put on trial at the Milimani Chief Magistrate’s Court. On July 30, 2021, the court delivered its judgment in Criminal Case No 13 of 2019, Republic v AAM, convicting him and sentencing him to life imprisonment.
Also read: When the danger comes through a child’s phone: One in five children exposed to sexual content online
Aggrieved by both his conviction and sentence, AAM appealed to the High Court at Milimani Law Courts, Nairobi. On June 16, 2023, the High Court set aside the life sentence and resentenced him to 30 years’ imprisonment, calculated from the date of his conviction.
“Thus, in my view, Section 329 of the Criminal Procedure Code gives judges and magistrates, in appropriate cases, [the discretion] to consider mitigation and mete out a sentence that fits the offence committed despite another sentence being provided for under the Act in which the offence is prescribed,” Judge D Kavedza observed in the judgment.
“In that regard, I find life imprisonment shatters all the hopes of the appellant for rehabilitation or having another chance to start afresh.”
The duty to report
The failure by any person to report a case of child abuse is itself defined as child abuse under the Children Act (Cap 141). Section 145 of the Act further states that a person who has reasonable cause to believe that a child is in need of care and protection may report the matter to the nearest authorised officer.
The authorised officer is then required to take the necessary steps to secure a court order for the care and protection of the child in a place of safety or other alternative care provided for under the Act. The law sets out various circumstances in which a child may be considered to require care and protection.
Also read: Rising child abuse demands urgent attention
These include children who have been sexually abused or are at risk of sexual abuse or exploitation, including prostitution or pornography. The law also protects children who have undergone or are at risk of female genital mutilation or forced male circumcision.
It covers children whose lives or safety are threatened by a family member, those who are victims of human trafficking, and those living in overcrowded, unhygienic or dangerous conditions. It also protects children who are exposed to violence, are pregnant or responsible for another child’s pregnancy, or are mentally or terminally ill.
Reporting is not limited to parents
The responsibility to report suspected abuse does not rest with parents alone. For instance, Mabera Sub-County Children’s Officer Janet Robi said she placed a girl under care after receiving a report of alleged defilement in June this year.
Janet said she first encountered the case while handling a separate matter involving an abandoned nine-month-old child. According to her, the mother of the abandoned child went to her office and alleged that an elderly man was defiling a 12-year-old girl.
“I took up the defilement case and referred it to the police gender desk for investigation, which prompted the arrest of the perpetrator,” she said.
As these cases show, teachers, health workers, relatives, neighbours, community volunteers and other concerned people can help connect children at risk with protection services and provide a pathway to justice for crimes committed against them.

title: En 2002, estudiantes de arquitectura de Alabama apilaron 72.000 baldosas de alfombra desgastadas en las paredes de una casa familiar; ahora Rural Studio ha construido más de 200 proyectos
content:
En Mason’s Bend, Alabama, una casa familiar quedó marcada por una idea tan simple como radical: usar baldosas de alfombra gastadas como si fueran ladrillos.
El proyecto se llama Lucy Carpet House y fue realizado en 2002 por estudiantes de Rural Studio, el programa de diseño y construcción de la Escuela de Arquitectura, Planificación y Arquitectura del Paisaje de Auburn University.
Según la ficha oficial de Rural Studio, la casa fue pensada para la familia Harris y sus muros contienen 72.000 baldosas individuales apiladas, sostenidas por compresión bajo una pesada viga de madera.
Una casa hecha con descarte industrial
El desafío nació de un patrocinio de Interface, fabricante de baldosas de alfombra. La consigna era aprovechar ese material usado en la construcción de una vivienda.
En vez de tratarlo como revestimiento, los estudiantes lo convirtieron en masa estructural: pieza sobre pieza, hasta formar paredes gruesas, densas y visualmente inconfundibles. Rural Studio aclara que las baldosas estuvieron almacenadas durante siete años antes de usarse, para asegurarse de que ya no liberaran gases residuales del material.
La casa combinó una lógica doméstica con una necesidad concreta del territorio: su torre contiene un dormitorio en la parte superior y un refugio contra tornados en la inferior.
La vivienda no fue solo una rareza arquitectónica. Rural Studio nació justamente para hacer de la construcción una forma de aprendizaje y servicio.
El programa trabaja en el Black Belt de Alabama, una región rural con necesidades históricas de vivienda, infraestructura y acceso a recursos básicos. Su misión, según la propia institución, combina educación de estudiantes, investigación sobre vida rural saludable y soluciones construidas junto a las comunidades.
Rural Studio, de experimento a modelo
Más de tres décadas después, la Lucy Carpet House aparece como una pieza dentro de una obra mucho más amplia. Rural Studio informa que ya construyó más de 220 proyectos y formó a más de 1.200 estudiantes en el Black Belt. Cada año, alrededor de cuatro decenas de alumnos participan de esta experiencia de aprendizaje situada, viviendo y trabajando cerca de las comunidades para las que diseñan.
El programa no se limita a viviendas. También desarrolló edificios cívicos, espacios comunitarios, investigaciones sobre vivienda accesible, sistemas de madera, agricultura de pequeña escala y acceso a agua limpia. En su propia definición, Rural Studio no les pregunta a los estudiantes únicamente qué se puede construir, sino qué debería construirse.
Aquella casa de 72.000 baldosas muestra una de las mejores intuiciones del programa: el diseño puede empezar donde otros ven descarte. En manos de estudiantes y docentes, una montaña de alfombra usada se convirtió en paredes, refugio, memoria material y una pregunta vigente sobre cómo construir mejor con lo que ya existe.

title: Noly Blak Distributes Thousands of Pesos to Those in Need in Holguín
content:
Humanitarian activist Norge Ernesto Díaz Blak, known as Noly Blak, took to the streets of Holguín with a backpack filled with over 600,000 pesos, distributing it to the sick, homeless, elderly, and families with hospitalized children. This act of kindness was documented on his Facebook profile.
The initiative began with a generous donation from a follower. "Adriani gave me 900 dollars. I sold it to distribute among the sick, the homeless, and those in need," Noly stated at the start of his video. After exchanging the dollars for Cuban pesos, he ventured out, determined to reach as many people as possible.
His first stop was a pediatric hospital in the city, where he handed out 20,000 pesos to each parent staying with their admitted children. These families came from distant municipalities like Calixto García, Mayarí, Rafael Freire, Marcané, Cacocum, and La Viajaca, having been at the medical center for days or even weeks.
Heartfelt Stories from Hospital Corridors
Every hallway held a story. One child suffered from renal tubular acidosis and diabetes insipidus; another family was in desperate need of a medication unavailable at the hospital. "Here, 20,000 pesos, it's not much, but it's from the heart of a friend of mine," Noly told one mother.
Nighttime Generosity in the Streets
As night fell, Noly continued his mission on the streets. Elderly individuals, people with physical disabilities, Cubans scavenging for items to sell, and those queuing outside a bank received sums ranging from 5,000 to 20,000 pesos, depending on their circumstances.
A particularly touching moment occurred when Noly met a father caring for his two daughters alone. "God willing, one day we'll have a home and rest under a roof," the man remarked upon receiving assistance.
The Ongoing Commitment to Community Aid
This act was not an isolated event. For years, Noly Blak has been building a community-driven solidarity network in Holguín, entirely funded by voluntary donations from Cubans both on the island and abroad. His project, "Casas para Cuba," has successfully constructed or repaired more than 20 homes for vulnerable families, including one for a mother with four children in Cacocum.
Earlier this year, in March, the activist distributed 65,000 pesos among beggars, the elderly, and the disabled on the streets of Holguín. In April, a campaign he initiated raised over three million pesos for a family in extreme poverty, and another in May collected more than a million pesos for two brothers from the Paraíso neighborhood. In September, he highlighted the case of Gretel, a young woman with paranoid schizophrenia confined in Velasco, Gibara, whose family tearfully appreciated the assistance.
Closing the video of this charitable outing, Noly expressed gratitude to the one who made it all possible: "Adrianys, thank you for helping me help. May God bless all my followers."
Frequently Asked Questions about Noly Blak's Humanitarian Efforts
Who is Noly Blak?
Noly Blak, whose real name is Norge Ernesto Díaz Blak, is a humanitarian activist known for his charitable initiatives in Holguín, Cuba.
What is "Casas para Cuba"?
"Casas para Cuba" is a project initiated by Noly Blak, aimed at constructing or repairing homes for vulnerable families in Cuba, funded through voluntary donations.
How does Noly Blak support those in need?
Noly Blak supports those in need through direct monetary distributions, community projects like building homes, and highlighting individual cases that require assistance.

title: Dry cleaner ‘damages’ her Pashmina clothes, Srinagar woman wins Rs 59,000 payout
content:
4 min readNew DelhiUpdated: Sep 23, 2026 04:46 PM IST

A Srinagar consumer commission has directed a dry-cleaning service to pay Rs 59,000 to a woman after her clothes, including a Pashmina shawl, were allegedly returned in a damaged condition. The woman had paid Rs 5,970 to have 18 items dry cleaned and claimed that the garments were damaged during the process.
President Dr Farah Deeba and member Shabnum Munshi, while hearing the complaint filed by the woman on September 19, noted that the dry cleaner admitted through WhatsApp messages that its workers had caused the damage and that its attempts to restore the clothes had failed.
“Verily, arrogance on the part of the opposite party (dry cleaner) not to respond to the complaint of the complainant would surely have caused serious mental pain, agony, harassment and financial loss to him. All these circumstances taken together would lead to the conclusion that such an act of the opposite party tantamounts to the deficiency of service,” the commission observed.




Received damaged clothes
The woman claimed that she came to know through advertisements about the dry-cleaning services and approached the service provider to dry clean 18 articles, including a Pashmina shawl and Pashmina pheran (loose tunic) worth over Rs 47,000. She said the dry cleaner assured her of the best possible service and charged Rs 5,970, which she paid on March 26, 2024.
The woman alleged that when the clothes, including the shawl and pheran, were returned after dry cleaning, they were damaged. She then approached the dry cleaner, who allegedly assured her that the shawl and pheran would either be replaced or their value would be paid to her.
However, despite repeated requests and a legal notice, the dry cleaner did not resolve her grievance. She then approached the commission, alleging that she had suffered mental pain, harassment and financial loss. The woman was represented by advocate B A Shah before the commission.
‘Damages couldn’t be restored’
The commission noted that the dry cleaner failed to contest the case or file its version before the commission and found that “ the opposite party (dry cleaner) has admitted in the WhatsApp chat with the complainant that the damage to the articles has been done by the workers while working with the opposite party.”
Story continues below this ad
It also found that the dry cleaner admitted that they tried to restore the damage caused to the clothes during the dry cleaning services, but they could not be restored.  Noting that the woman had claimed the cost of the clothes damaged to be Rs 47,000, it held that the dry cleaner was deficient in providing service and that the woman had suffered mental pain, agony, harassment and financial loss.
The commission directed the dry cleaner to pay Rs 47,000 for the damaged clothes, Rs 10,000 as compensation, and Rs 2,000 as litigation costs, for a total of Rs 59,000.
Takeaway
This ruling highlights that dry-cleaning services can be held liable when clothes are damaged during the service.
For consumer-related grievances, individuals may contact the consumer helpline in their respective states (Jammu and Kashmir Consumer Commission Helpline: 1800 180 7114) or call the National Consumer Helpline at 1915 for assistance.

title: Kyrgyzstan’s Nomad Games bring traditional sports to global stage
content:
The Nomad Games, held every two years, have grown since their inaugural edition in 2014, drawing more than 3,000 athletes to Kyrgyzstan this year, organisers said.
The mountainous Central Asian country of seven million was the birthplace of the games and retains a strong popular following for many of the sports, which have deep roots across the region.
“These games have the nomadic spirit,” said Mumina Daminova, a horseback archer from Uzbekistan, who competed in flowing white traditional robes.
“It’s like Olympic games but for ethnosport,” she said.
The event also attracts competitors from countries without a history of nomadism, including Britain, whose athletes took part in horseback archery and tug of war.
London-based executive coach Becca Sweetman has competed in horseback archery for the Great Britain team for the past eight years, after a friend introduced her to the sport.
“About eight years ago a friend asked if I wanted to have a go at horseback archery and I just got hooked on this amazing sport,” she said.
Sam Pollard, a London-based consultant, joined Britain’s tug of war team after becoming interested in the games through videos of Kok Boru, a nomadic sport similar to polo that uses a sheep carcass instead of a ball.
“That looks awesome,” he said, adding that the timing of the games also suited his plans to visit Central Asia.
While international participation has expanded, the games remain particularly significant in countries such as Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia and the other Central Asian republics, where traditional nomadic sports continue to draw large followings.
The opening ceremony in Bishkek was attended by leaders including Russian President Vladimir Putin, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan and India’s Narendra Modi, who were in the Kyrgyz capital for a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.

title: From 33 to 12 hours, 14 to 6: Vande Bharat, roads cutting travel time drastically
content:
India’s infrastructure expansion has been continuing for several years now, with the fruits of the labour now visible in terms of less travel time between places. Across bridges, tunnels, expressways and railways, projects are replacing long detours, difficult terrain and slower routes with more direct connections.
The latest government factsheet brings together examples of how these investments are changing journey times across the country.
Bridges: Crossing barriers, cutting hours
Bridges have made some of the biggest differences where rivers and difficult crossings once added hours to a journey. The Bhupen Hazarika Setu, or Dhola-Sadiya Bridge, reduced travel time between Rupai in Assam and Meka/Roing in Arunachal Pradesh from six hours to one hour. The Bogibeel Bridge brought the journey between Dhemaji and Dibrugarh down from almost an entire day to around one to two hours.
The gains are equally striking elsewhere. The Atal Setu has cut the Mumbai-Navi Mumbai journey from about two hours to around 20 minutes, while the Kosi Rail Mahasetu reduced the Nirmali-Saraigarh rail journey from eight hours to 30 minutes and shortened the distance from around 300 km to 22 km.
Tunnels: Taking the shorter route through mountains
Tunnels are changing travel in areas where geography has traditionally been a major constraint. The 9.02-km Atal Tunnel bypasses Rohtang Pass, cuts 46 km from the Manali-Sarchu route and saves four to five hours.
The Dr Syama Prasad Mookerjee Tunnel reduces the Jammu-Srinagar travel distance by about 30 km and saves nearly two hours.
The Banihal-Qazigund twin-tube tunnel saves around one and a half hours, while the Sela Tunnel in Arunachal Pradesh has reduced travel time on the Tezpur-Tawang route by more than an hour and provides all-weather connectivity.
Expressways: Compressing long road journeys
Access-controlled highways are producing similar reductions on major road routes. The Delhi-Meerut Expressway has brought the journey down from around two and a half hours to 50 minutes. Bengaluru-Mysuru has fallen from nearly three hours to about 75 minutes, while the Delhi-Dehradun Economic Corridor has reduced travel time from more than six hours to around two and a half hours.
The Delhi-Amritsar-Katra Expressway aims to cut Delhi-Amritsar travel from eight hours to four hours and Delhi-Katra travel from 14 hours to six hours. The Delhi-Mumbai Expressway is being developed to bring the journey down from roughly 33 hours to about 12 hours.
Railways: Making conventional trains faster
The speed gains are not limited to new railway lines. The 2026 railway timetable has speeded up 549 trains across the network. Of these, 20 trains gained at least 60 minutes, 48 gained 31-59 minutes, 105 gained 16-30 minutes and another 376 were made five to 15 minutes faster.
Vande Bharat services have added another layer to this effort. The New Delhi-Varanasi service is around 40-50% faster than earlier services on the route. The Katra-Srinagar service saves two to three hours, while the Banaras-Khajuraho train saves around two hours and 40 minutes. The Ernakulam-Bengaluru service saves more than two hours.
The Vande Bharat Sleeper between Howrah and Guwahati has reduced the journey from around 17 hours to about 14 hours and has 16 air-conditioned coaches carrying around 823 passengers.
High-speed rail: The next connectivity leap
The next stage is high-speed rail. The 508-km Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail Corridor is designed for an operational speed of 320 kmph and is expected to bring the journey down to around one hour and 58 minutes. It will have 12 stations and include India's first undersea rail tunnel, around 7 km beneath Thane Creek.
The government has also announced seven high-speed rail corridors covering nearly 4,000 km, with estimated investment of Rs 16 lakh crore. The proposed routes include Delhi-Varanasi, Varanasi-Patna-Siliguri, Chennai-Bengaluru, Bengaluru-Hyderabad, Chennai-Hyderabad, Mumbai-Pune and Pune-Hyderabad.

title: No Longer “Untreatable”: Alzheimer’s Breakthroughs Are on the Horizon, Report Finds
content:
The World Alzheimer Report 2026 contains some encouraging news about the devastating neurodegenerative disorder, namely that we’re on a path to making Alzheimer’s a treatable condition.
“After decades of investment in research, we stand on the cusp of a giant leap forward at the intersection of innovation in diagnostics, treatments, and risk reduction,” Chris Lynch, the acting CEO of Alzheimer’s Disease International, wrote in the report, released Monday. He added:
“Never before has there been so much focus, investment, and hope in dementia research.”
Already, certain drugs (donanemab and lecanemab) have shown promise in slowing the progression of Alzheimer’s — and research is underway to find out if early treatment for high-risk individuals can alter the disease course before symptoms even develop. The report also flagged the potential for tailoring medical treatments to specific patients within the next five years.
“The mood across the research community is infectious,” it stated. “Alzheimer’s disease is no longer universally described as untreatable; instead, it is increasingly viewed as a condition for which earlier diagnosis, better understanding of disease biology, and a wider range of interventions may collectively improve outcomes.” This optimistic shift comes at a pivotal time, as the number of people living with dementia is projected to surpass 139 million by 2050.
Neurologist Campbell Le Heron agreed that the report signals a shift in mentality about the disease, away from something “that we can’t do anything about,” he told Radio New Zealand. He added: “These trials are showing us that we can potentially do something about it, at least in certain situations.”
The report also noted that, in addition to the drugs created specifically for Alzheimer’s, more research is being undertaken to explore the prospect of repurposing different medicines for treatment. “More than a third of dementia drugs currently in the pipeline were originally developed for other conditions,” it reads, citing atomoxetine as an example, a drug used to treat ADHD and formerly sold under the brand name Strattera. In a Phase 2 trial, scientists investigated “whether it could slow cognitive decline in people with mild cognitive impairment or early Alzheimer’s disease, with mixed results.”
Overall, “dementia is being recast not as a gradual decline towards an inevitable loss of cognition,” the researchers wrote, “but as a continuum that might be interrupted or slowed, enabling many more years with a good quality of life.”

title: In Allahabad High Court: Illegal detention, Rs 50,000 payout and praise for police officer
content:
4 min readNew DelhiSep 21, 2026 05:26 PM IST

Praising a senior Uttar Pradesh police officer for admitting an “error” on the part of the police over a man’s illegal detention in August, the Allahabad High Court has awarded Rs 50,000 compensation to the man and ordered his release.
“…this Court wishes to record its appreciation for the candour with which Mr. Vivek Chandra Yadav, Deputy Commissioner of Police has disclosed unequivocally in his affidavit without trying to beat around the bush and accepting the error on the part of the police without any ambiguity,” the court said.
A division bench of Justices Atul Sreedharan and Achal Sachdev passed the order on September 18 while hearing a habeas corpus petition filed by a man, who alleged that he had been illegally detained by the police.




“This Court unhesitatingly holds that the petitioner was held in illegal custody from 15.08.2026 till he was produced before the Magistrate and sent to judicial remand on 19.08.2026,” the order read.
Justices Atul Sreedharan and Achal Sachdev passed the order on September 18 while hearing a habeas corpus petition filed by a man.
According to the plea, the petitioner was allegedly picked up from his shop by two armed policemen on August 15. The court had earlier sought the personal affidavit of the Superintendent of Police after reference was made to CCTV footage of the incident.
The Deputy Commissioner of Police, in his affidavit, told the court that the petitioner had a property dispute with his neighbour, who levelled a serious allegation against him of being a citizen of Bangladesh and filed a police complaint against the petitioner. The high court made it clear that it was not examining the merits of those allegations and was concerned only with the legality of his custody.
It was further stated in the affidavit that the petitioner was picked up from his medical shop on August 15 and sent to jail on August 19. The deputy commissioner of police told the court that the Station House Officer and the investigating officer had failed to give a satisfactory explanation for the petitioner’s detention from August 15. Both officers were suspended on September 17 for gross negligence.
Story continues below this ad
The SHO claimed that he had instructed two constables to ask the petitioner to report to the police station, but they misunderstood the instructions and took him along with them. The SHO also said that he had been away from the police station on August 15 following a firing incident in the area.
The court thus held that the petitioner had been kept in illegal custody from August 15 until his production before the magistrate and subsequent remand on August 19. It ordered that he be released forthwith, unless he was wanted in any other case. The court clarified that the order would not prevent the State from arresting him again if necessary, provided the procedure established by law was followed.
The bench further directed the State to pay Rs 50,000 as compensation for the illegal detention. The amount is to be recovered from those found responsible after an inquiry.
The court appreciated the Deputy Commissioner of Police for acknowledging the police error and directed that the officer’s conduct be placed on his service record. It similarly appreciated the SHO’s disclosure of the circumstances leading to the illegal detention.
Story continues below this ad
“The Court hopes that the police would take cognizance and carry out corrective measures in future, so that such incidents may not happen, while the requirement of an accused in the investigative process is also fulfilled and his constitutional rights are also taken into cognizance,” the order read.

Yasmin, who declined to reveal the child’s gender, said: “Rather than having to uncover these concerns from scratch, the information (from the unit) helped us focus on key risks early and respond in a timely manner.”
The family service centre drew up a plan to keep the child safe, which includes getting the relatives, the child’s school and healthcare partners to look out for and support the child.
It also managed to get the family to agree to “non-negotiables” such as not using physical force to discipline the child, and ensuring the child is not exposed to the parents’ fights.
Yasmin said the child is no longer harshly punished physically, and the family continues to receive support from the centre.
On Sept 22, the new unit, called SAFER (Sensemaking Alerts for Frontline Engagement and Response), was launched to strengthen the child protection system in the wake of Megan Khung’s death.
Megan, who was four, had been abused by her mother and the woman’s former boyfriend for over a year before she died in 2020, in a case that drew public scrutiny and numerous questions in Parliament.
An independent review of her case found multiple breaches across agencies, including a Child Protective Service officer failing to log a call by Megan’s pre-school seeking help and police officers not following procedures.
And none of the agencies pieced together the various calls or information to form a fuller picture of the danger that Megan was in, until it was too late.
SAFER is designed to address this gap.
For a start, the unit analyses information given by the Central Narcotics Bureau, the police and MSF agencies, such as the National Anti-Violence and Sexual Harassment Helpline and the Early Childhood Development Agency, for families with children below seven years old where there are child protection concerns.
An MSF spokesperson told The Straits Times that SAFER uses a risk algorithm based on data analytics to combine information from available datasets, including recent stressors or risk events, to assess the family’s potential needs.
Trained professionals would review any potential child protection concerns, check against available facts of the case, consult existing case managers, and use their professional judgment to decide the next course of action.
Social service professionals welcomed the alerts provided by SAFER, as the families they work with often do not reveal – or may even hide – critical information about developments in the family or about family members.
Some of these facts are hard for social workers to uncover even after they do their due diligence.
Yet, such developments may place children at greater risk of harm, such as if a parent is known to have a drug habit, which could affect their ability to look after children.
Steven Tham, executive director of Good News Family Service Centre, said some families feel embarrassed or ashamed to reveal certain information.
Jeff Tan, centre head of THK Family Service Centre@Tanjong Pagar, said some families are also afraid that the information they share may be used against them, so they remain tight-lipped.
With SAFER giving a fuller picture of what is happening in a family, social workers say they are better able to understand the family’s situation, assess the risks and come up with a stronger plan to keep the children safe.
Yasmin said: “SAFER allows us to identify emerging risks earlier, recognise patterns that may otherwise remain hidden, and engage families with the right support before concerns escalate into more serious child safety issues.”
Good News Family Service Centre was able to provide more targeted support for a family with three young children after it was alerted to the case.
The children’s mother, who is divorced from their father, was struggling with communicating with them and managing their behaviour. She also has financial woes and did not want to talk about her former husband at all.
SAFER alerted the family service centre that the children’s father had broken the law, the details of which were not shared with ST.
Upon learning this fact and talking to the children, the family service centre’s staff realised the influence the father had on them, which might have contributed to the issues the mother had with them.
Tham said: “We have to help the children understand right from wrong. Once we knew where the influence was coming from, we can try to address this.”
Social workers added that many of the families they work with struggle with multiple and complex problems, such as financial difficulties, mental health conditions, relationship conflicts and caregiving stress.
Such problems may strain their ability to cope with the demands of life or look after their children adequately, they said.
While responding to alerts sent by SAFER may require more attention and work, Yasmin said it is a valuable resource.
She added: “Even when a concern does not materialise into significant risk, the act of checking reinforces our commitment to early intervention and safeguarding children before harm occurs.”

title: PPCRV resumes operations, aims to finish auditing BARMM polls ERs
content:
PPCRV resumes operations, aims to finish auditing BARMM polls ERs
MANILA, Philippines – The Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV) resumed its operations to audit the election returns (ERs) for the first Bangsamoro parliamentary elections on Sept. 23, at the AMA Makati Medical Annex Building.
PPCRV spokesperson Ana Singson said the election watchdog aims to finish auditing the remaining 2,700 ERs by the end of the day.
“Our average per day is 1,000. Today, we have to finish 2,700. So I said, ‘All hands on deck,’” Singson said.
The election watchdog expanded its volunteer workforce on Wednesday, including students from AMA and PPCRV volunteers. It also converted other rooms into scanning centers to accommodate the increased workload.
PPCRV double-checks the votes transmitted by the automated counting machines against the physical ERs to ensure there are no discrepancies in the data.
Singson told the Inquirer that no significant discrepancies had been observed as of Wednesday. Most of the flagged discrepancies were due to scanning issues, which were resolved by rescanning the physical ERs.
However, PPCRV continues to discover ERs with strips in the middle. As of this writing, nearly 2 percent of the ERs have been found to have such issues.
READ: PPCRV flags unreadable election returns in BARMM polls
PPCRV collected around 4,700 of the 5,212 ERs, representing more than 90 percent of the total. Singson noted that the figure was “very high” compared with previous elections.
“That’s high. Usually in our national coverage, we can only get 60 percent. [The number 90 percent] shows you how great the coordinators are,” Singson told the Inquirer.
She added that this was the “highest-ever average,” reflecting the massive effort of the volunteers.
The remaining ERs were brought in on Tuesday by Fr. Dave Procalia, PPCRV’s head of operations in the Bangsamoro region.
“[Fr. Dave] carried 29 kilos worth of ERs, equivalent to 2,377 ERs from BARMM, SHA, Ampatuan area and the rest of the balance,” Singson said.
Another 300 physical ERs from Lanao del Sur are expected to arrive within the day, Singson said. /jpv

title: Počinje isplata 6.000 dinara: Ko danas dobija novac, a ko mora da sačeka do sutra
content:
Isplata jednokratne pomoći od 6.000 dinara biće sprovedena tokom četiri dana, a trebalo bi da bude završena u petak. Ko novac dobija danas, ko od 23. septembra i ko nije morao da se prijavi?
Isplata jednokratne pomoći od 6.000 dinara počinje danas, 22. septembra, a novac će građanima biti uplaćivan u naredna četiri dana. Prvi na redu su građani koji pravo ostvaruju preko Akcionarskog fonda, kao i penzioneri i korisnici novčane socijalne pomoći, dok će oni koji su se za pomoć prijavljivali preko portala Uprave za trezor novac početi da dobijaju od srede.
Prema podacima Banke Poštanska štedionica, danas će biti obuhvaćeno oko 4,3 miliona građana koji pravo ostvaruju preko Akcionarskog fonda, kao i oko 575.000 ljudi koji pravo na pomoć ostvaruju po zakonu, a nisu imali obavezu da se prijavljuju.
Do ponoći 21. septembra za pomoć od 6.000 dinara prijavilo se oko 1,7 miliona građana.
Isplata u naredna četiri dana
Prema planu isplate, u sredu, 23. septembra, novac će biti uplaćen za gotovo milion građana koji su se prijavljivali za pomoć.
Za četvrtak, 24. septembar, predviđena je isplata za još oko 500.000 ljudi, među kojima su građani koji su se prijavili poslednjeg dana roka.
Isplata bi trebalo da bude završena u petak, 25. septembra.
Punoletni građani koji nisu nosioci prava po osnovu besplatnih akcija, a koji su se prijavili preko portala Uprave za trezor, pomoć dobijaju u okviru ovog ciklusa isplate.
Penzioneri, korisnici novčane socijalne pomoći i određene druge kategorije građana obuhvaćene zakonom nisu morali da podnose prijavu za 6.000 dinara.
Njima se novac uplaćuje na osnovu podataka iz državnih evidencija.
Automatska isplata predviđena je i za lica koja se nalaze u zavodima za izvršenje krivičnih sankcija.
Pravo na novac imaju i naslednici preminulih građana koji su imali besplatne akcije. Za isplatu je potrebno pravosnažno rešenje o nasleđivanju i važeća lična karta, dok se novac isplaćuje preko Banke Poštanska štedionica.
Koliko dugo može da se podigne novac
Za građane koji pomoć ostvaruju iz Akcionarskog fonda ne postoji rok za podizanje novca.
Kod građana koji 6.000 dinara dobijaju iz državnog budžeta, novac će biti moguće podići u roku od godinu dana.
Građanima koji nemaju račun u banci za ovu namenu biće otvoren račun u Banci Poštanska štedionica.
Šta je potrebno za prijavu
Građani koji su morali da se prijave za pomoć svoj status su mogli da provere i prijavu podnesu preko portala Uprave za trezor.
Prilikom provere bilo je potrebno uneti matični broj i broj lične karte. Rok za prijavljivanje istekao je 21. septembra u ponoć.
Jednokratna pomoć od 6.000 dinara deo je šireg paketa državne pomoći koji, prema podacima Ministarstva finansija, obuhvata različite kategorije građana i ukupno je vredan gotovo milijardu evra.

title: ¿Por qué en Carora el exalcalde fue perseguido? La historia comienza en 2024
content:
¿Por qué en Carora el exalcalde fue perseguido? La historia comienza en 2024
Ante un padrón electoral dominado por mujeres en el municipio Torres de Lara, correspondiente a Carora, vecinas de distintas trayectorias se capacitaron para convertirse en defensoras clave del sufragio y resguardar las actas electorales del 28 de julio. Luego de aquellos comicios, se registró un aumento de acciones represivas que terminaron en la imputación del entonces alcalde Javier Oropeza y de otras personas de su círculo cercano
Yoselin Álvarez | Redsonadoras
Meses antes de las elecciones presidenciales de 2024 en Venezuela, en la ciudad de Carora, capital del municipio Torres del estado Lara, se tejía una sólida red para defender la voluntad popular que se manifestó a través del voto. Sus protagonistas fueron mujeres que se prepararon para contribuir a la construcción del país con el que sueñan.
Este movimiento nació, originalmente, de un espacio de resistencia gremial, de un grupo de trabajadoras del sector educativo que se reunían para exigir salarios dignos, la restitución de los contratos colectivos y el cese de la política de bonificación del ingreso. Sin embargo, en medio de esos debates, la conversación dio un giro decisivo: para transformar sus condiciones laborales era imprescindible incidir en el poder.
Así fue como el grupo decidió abrir sus puertas a amas de casa, militantes de organizaciones políticas e integrantes de la sociedad civil en general. Mediante talleres, asambleas y charlas formativas comenzaron a capacitarse en la defensa del derecho al sufragio, aprendiendo que el voto es una herramienta para influir en la toma de decisiones locales, regionales y nacionales.
El objetivo final apuntó a fortalecer la participación política de las mujeres en los 138 centros de votación del municipio Torres, donde 75 % del padrón electoral está conformado por mujeres, según los últimos datos disponibles del Consejo Nacional Electoral (CNE). Buscaban garantizar que sus voces realmente se escucharan en un contexto político complejo.
En estos espacios, mujeres de distintas edades y con diferentes historias consolidaron redes de apoyo, compartieron experiencias, discutieron los retos que enfrentan a diario y planificaron acciones conjuntas. Ahí germinó un sentido de comunidad y solidaridad.
El grupo creció entre colegas educadoras, amigas, familiares, con las que, aún dos años después, comparten como una gran familia. Ahora la red está formada por profesionales en diversas carreras y oficios, pero también por mujeres que no tuvieron acceso a la educación y ahora se sienten escuchadas.
El paso a un liderazgo activo
“Nos preparamos para ser parte de lo que soñamos”, contó Marileyda Rojas, licenciada en educación inicial e integrante del partido político Encuentro Ciudadano, al recordar su experiencia formativa en este movimiento de mujeres.
La educadora admitió que antes de estos espacios no se sentía capaz de lograr muchas cosas en su vida, que tenía una actitud más sumisa. “Actualmente me siento una líder; estoy fortalecida porque sé que aporto mi grano de arena para la libertad de este país”.
Para Marlene Pérez, secretaria de la Escuela Bolivariana Priscilo Véliz desde hace 30 años, la motivación de participar en este grupo y por esa causa fue querer el bienestar de sus hijos y de toda su familia. “El padrón electoral lo conformamos en su mayoría mujeres. Nos sentimos identificadas con la necesidad de un cambio y somos responsables al momento de tomar decisiones”, dijo.
Ella se siente protagonista de esas transformaciones que ha habido en el país, particularmente desde el 3 de enero de 2026. Opinó que aunque lentos, son un avance significativo y que sin duda tienen su antecedente en el 28 de julio de 2024: “Fui coordinadora de uno de los centros electorales y al momento de tomar decisiones somos aguerridas. Las mujeres tenemos un control que nadie logra”.
Pérez relató que antes de este evento electoral, la mayoría de mujeres que ahora son parte de la red desconocían sus derechos, y el poder transformador del que ahora son conscientes. “Nos acostumbraron a hacer las tareas del hogar, nos limitaron a cumplir con la casa, la familia, pero no nos dijeron lo que podemos lograr a través de nuestra participación activa en la toma de decisiones de un país”.
Ahora, con una certeza inquebrantable y una fe intacta, se mantiene de pie junto al gran grupo que se ha logrado conformar.
Resguardar las actas del 28 de julio
Para muchas de estas mujeres lo que vivieron aquel 28 de julio de 2024 era un trabajo totalmente desconocido. El rol que jugaron durante aquella jornada fue fundamental: resguardaron las actas electorales que luego la oposición venezolana difundió como una prueba del triunfo de Edmundo González Urrutia, aunque el CNE había nombrado a Nicolás Maduro como ganador. En Carora, entonces, hubo protestas por aquellos anuncios.
Sobre aquel día las mujeres de Carora recordaron, por ejemplo, cómo se blindaron. Tenían nombres, fotos y referencias de quiénes irían a los centros de votación para recoger las copias físicas de las actas que imprimían directamente las máquinas de votación. Tenían grupos de WhatsApp donde se comunicaban constantemente y verificaban cada paso del proceso: no hacían la entrega hasta tanto tener la confirmación de que era la persona correcta.
Todo el trabajo que hicieron, sin embargo, enfrentó una fuerte repercusión apenas horas después de que el Poder Electoral anunciara sus resultados. Ahí comenzó la pesadilla para muchas. Noches de insomnio, desespero y zozobra debido a la persecución que emprendió el Gobierno de Maduro contra la disidencia.
Tras la activación de la llamada “Operación tun-tun”, hombres vestidos de negro que llegaban a las viviendas de las señaladas como “traidoras a la patria”. Las amedrentaban y, en algunos casos, las llevaban detenidas.
“Los días se hicieron largos, el temor de salir a la calle se incrementó con el correr de las horas. La comunicación entre familiares, amigos y la estructura del partido era casi nula, ya que desconocíamos si había alguna interferencia en nuestros equipos celulares”, contó una de las integrantes del grupo.
Otras de las mujeres del movimiento narraron cómo cambiaron sus rutinas. Solo salían a la calle a hacer diligencias puntuales, no confiaban en sus vecinos, temían por su vida y la de sus hijos. La incertidumbre era mayor con el pasar del tiempo.
“Nos comunicábamos con mensajes que se autodestruyen. Yo no dormía. Me mantenía alerta porque las detenciones no paraban”, agregó otra de las entrevistadas. Para protegerse evitaban a toda costa estar en lugares públicos: “Nos enmudecieron por un tiempo, del tema no se hablaba, solo se pensaba porque decirlo se convertía en un arma para que te acusaran de incitación al odio”.
Persecución que dio pie al exilio
Tras las protestas postelectorales que se desataron en varios estados del país, el alcalde opositor de Carora, Javier Oropeza, fue víctima de una fuerte persecución y decidió huir del país junto a su familia.
Iraida Timaure, quien formaba parte del gabinete de Oropeza, fue nombrada alcaldesa encargada. Sin embargo, el acoso y el asedio por parte del Ejecutivo nacional también la alcanzó e igualmente tuvo que exiliarse. La acusaron, sin pruebas, de una serie de delitos. Además, allanaron su vivienda y el Estado venezolano confiscó sus bienes.
Otro caso emblemático de esta persecución en Carora fue la detención de Yenny Lucía Barrios, militante de Voluntad Popular, defensora de derechos humanos y de los animales, y una mujer destacada en la sociedad caroreña. La lideresa padecía linfoma no Hodgkin y su salud ya estaba comprometida cuando la apresaron el 9 de septiembre de 2024 y la trasladaron a una cárcel en la ciudad de Barquisimeto.
Su arresto generó consternación entre amigos, familiares y allegados. La acusaron de terrorismo e instigación al odio. Gracias a la lucha de organizaciones defensoras de DDHH nacionales e internacionales, se logró que la excarcelaran el 11 de diciembre, pero con una medida de presentación ante los tribunales.
Poco después la familia recibió otro golpe: detuvieron al hijo de Yenny, Diego Sierralta, cuando intercambiaba unos medicamentos que su madre no necesitaba por otros que sí. En ese entonces, ella estaba recibiendo un segundo ciclo de quimioterapias. Al joven lo acusaron de tráfico de medicinas.
Yenny murió el 5 de noviembre del año 2025 por complicaciones asociadas al cáncer, muy afectada además por la detención de su hijo. A Diego lo excarcelaron el 6 de noviembre, un día después de la muerte de su madre, para que asistiera a su funeral.
Pese a las heridas de ese duro momento, muchas de las integrantes del movimiento en Carora piensan que salieron fortalecidas. Opinaron que incluso Barrios murió con la certeza de que trabajó por la libertad de Venezuela y la defensa del voto de la ciudadanía.
La fuerza, resiliencia y las ganas de darle un giro a la historia democrática de un país, llevó a estas mujeres a ser parte de lo que ahora definen como una “masa inquebrantable”. Sin embargo, reconocen que la sombra de la persecución sigue al acecho.
Luego de meses en el exilio, tanto el exalcalde de Carora Javier Oropeza como Iraida Timaure decidieron regresar a Venezuela con la esperanza de retomar sus espacios; pero la vulnerabilidad a la que aún están expuestos quedó en evidencia este jueves, 17 de septiembre, cuando hombres vestidos de negro a bordo de una camioneta negra se llevaron a Javier Oropeza cuando salía de una entrevista en el diario El Informador en Barquisimeto, según denunciaron testigos.
Oropeza fue capturado por efectivos de la División de Inteligencia Estratégica (DIE) de la PNB en Barquisimeto, organismo que lo trasladó al Palacio de Justicia, desde donde fue excarcelado a las 9:14 de la noche. El proceso judicial en su contra continúa.
*Lea también: Tras más de ocho horas detenido, exalcalde de Carora Javier Oropeza es excarcelado
*El periodismo en Venezuela se ejerce en un entorno hostil para la prensa con decenas de instrumentos jurídicos dispuestos para el castigo de la palabra, especialmente las leyes «contra el odio», «contra el fascismo» y «contra el bloqueo». Este contenido fue escrito tomando en consideración las amenazas y límites que, en consecuencia, se han impuesto a la divulgación de informaciones desde dentro del país.

title: Nigerian, British forwards granted Vietnamese citizenship
content:
The Ho Chi Minh City Department of Justice on Friday afternoon presented the two players with decisions by the Vietnamese State President granting them citizenship.
Olaha, born in 1997, has taken the Vietnamese name Olaha Manh Duc, while Lee, born in 2007, is now Williams Minh Hoang.
Speaking at the ceremony, Olaha said becoming a Vietnamese citizen had been a long-held dream since he first came to the country to play football.
“I am very happy and delighted to become a Vietnamese citizen,” he said. “I deeply appreciate everyone who has helped me make this dream come true. I promise to give my all to Cong An Ho Chi Minh City FC and Vietnamese football.”
The 1.86-meter-tall striker scored nine goals in 26 V-League appearances for Song Lam Nghe An last season before joining Cong An Ho Chi Minh City FC ahead of the 2026-27 campaign.
Williams Minh Hoang, meanwhile, scored six goals in 17 V-League matches for Cong An Ho Chi Minh City FC in the 2025-26 season.
The 1.9-meter forward also netted twice in three National Cup appearances, helping the club win the competition.
“I am very happy and honored to be granted Vietnamese citizenship,” Williams said after the ceremony. “I cannot thank enough everyone who has accompanied and helped me reach this milestone.”
Their naturalization allows Cong An Ho Chi Minh City FC to register both players as domestic footballers, giving the club more attacking options for the new V-League season.
The move could also strengthen Vietnam’s national-team pool.
Williams has already earned his first call-up, with head coach Kim Sang Sik including him in a 23-man squad announced Thursday for the upcoming FIFA ASEAN Cup 2026 in Indonesia.
He was one of two overseas Vietnamese players receiving their first call-ups, alongside France-born defender Nguyen Adou Leygley Minh.
Kim named five forwards in the squad: Williams, Nguyen Xuan Son, Nguyen Tai Loc, Dinh Bac, and Pham Gia Hung.
Xuan Son and Tai Loc are also naturalized Vietnamese players of Brazilian origin.

title: A meal in the fields: Savoring rice in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta
content:
A distinctive tradition among farmers in Vietnam's Mekong Delta is to provide meals for people hired to work in the fields, whether they are day laborers or workers hired for specific tasks.
Rather than returning home for lunch, everyone often eats together right there in the rice fields, under the open sky, turning a simple midday meal into part of the farming tradition.
Out in the fields, a meal is meant to be shared
'Com cay,' or field meal, refers to simple field meals prepared at home and carried out to the rice fields for people working there.
The food was often eaten quickly in the middle of the fields, under the open sky, before farmers returned to planting or other work.
The tradition grew out of the way rice was once grown in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta, one of the country’s most important rice-producing regions.
Farmers would first grow rice seedlings in one area. Once the seedlings were ready, they would pull them from the ground and transplant them by hand into another field.
During planting season, farmers often hired workers to help with the labor-intensive process.
The person who provided the work would also provide their meals, giving rise to the name 'field meal,' literally referring to the meals brought out to those doing the rice transplanting.
Le Duc Chi, a resident of Ca Mau Province, remembers the tradition from his childhood.
His uncle once owned more than 100 units of farmland, and nearby Khmer women would come to work as rice planters.
They were paid in advance and returned during planting season to work in the fields.
Chi was often the one responsible for bringing their meals.
“I used to bring food out to the field for the rice planters. That was what we called 'com cay,’” Chi said.
The work could begin long before sunrise.
When there was enough moonlight, workers sometimes started at 2:00 or 3:00 am, pulling seedlings from the ground and planting them row by row.
By the time the sun rose and the heat became intense, they could already have finished their assigned work.
If heavy rain or extreme heat stopped them during the day, they would take a break and make up the work later.
Preparing the meals was a job in itself.
Chi’s aunt would wake before dawn to cook for dozens of workers. When the sun came up, she would load the food onto a small boat, and Chi would row it out through the fields.
For families without a boat, there were other ways to get lunch to the workers.
Some carried the meal in baskets or large bags, while others built simple shoulder poles to carry the food, bowls and chopsticks out to the fields.
The result was a distinctly Mekong Delta scene: a home-cooked meal arriving by boat in the middle of a rice field, with farmers sitting down together under the sun before returning to work.
What might look unusual to an outsider was once an ordinary part of life for generations of rice farmers.
Some of the rice-growing steps once practiced by farmers in southern Vietnam, from soaking seeds to sprout, to sowing, pulling up seedlings and transplanting them. Photo: Ngo Hoang Vu
A humble feast by the rice fields
There was nothing elaborate about a 'com cay' meal.
Farmers ate whatever was available, often taking a short break after eating before returning to work. If the day’s work was finished early, they could head home early too.
There was no dining table. Meals were set down wherever the work happened, on the edge of a rice field, under a tree or beside a pond.
Banana leaves, sacks or the lids of containers could become makeshift tables. Sometimes, nothing was used at all. If there was food to eat, that was enough.
In some fields, the narrow strips of land between rice paddies were too small to sit on.
When the fields were deep and waterlogged, workers would stand in the water while eating, with the food placed on the bank.
“When I brought the food out to the field, everyone would call to one another to wash their hands and come eat,” Le Duc Chi recalled.
A typical meal consisted of just a few dishes, depending on what was available that day.
There was little expectation that the person providing the meal had to serve anything fancy.
Salty dishes were common because they helped replenish salt lost through heavy sweating during physical work.
The food could include fermented fish cooked with eggs, braised fish, dried fish, salty fried shrimp, boiled vegetables, eggs with preserved radish and a simple mixed-vegetable soup.
And sometimes, the fields themselves supplied the main dish.
If workers caught a snakehead fish while pulling up rice seedlings, they could roast it over rice straw or dried grass and eat it right away.
Others might pick water spinach, water mimosa, water lily stems or bitter greens growing nearby, wash them and dip them straight into fish sauce.
These simple meals carried the smells of the countryside with them, muddy water, fresh rice seedlings and ripening rice mixing with the scent of freshly cooked food.
For those eating, the combination could make an ordinary bowl of rice taste unforgettable.
On some days, field meal was even simpler: sticky rice cooked with beans, topped with sesame salt or crushed peanut salt.
There was no elaborate preparation, no proper table and no special occasion, just food, the people who worked the fields and a meal shared in the middle of the countryside.
Why simple can taste so good?
The meal was simple, yet everyone seemed to relish it.
The pleasure did not end when the meal was over. Even years later, those who once shared these field meals still remember them as delicious, although, as one person put it, “I don’t even know why they tasted so good.”
Han Ai Tien, former editor-in-chief of Bac Lieu newspaper, offered an explanation.
“Farmers had to wake up in the middle of the night or early in the morning and travel to the fields, sometimes going a long way. Then they would spend hours doing hard physical work," he said.
“By the time the meal arrived, they were extremely hungry. And the meal itself was a joyful occasion. Sometimes 10 or 20 people would sit down together, talking and laughing," he explained.
"Eating out in the fields also created a different atmosphere from eating at home. There was a sense of community, neighbors working and eating together, looking out over what they had accomplished in the fields. Perhaps that is where the food tasted so good," he said.
Today, as workers from the Mekong Delta increasingly move to cities for jobs, the large gatherings once associated with these field meals have become less common.
Families now tend to arrange their own work, while those who hire workers often pay them extra to cover their meals instead of preparing food for them.
The arrangement is more convenient for workers, who can bring whatever food they prefer. It also saves employers the time and effort of preparing meals for a group.
People in the Mekong Delta still bring food with them when they work in their fields and gardens, but the meals are usually smaller and more informal.
“These field meals are a reminder of a land that was both fertile and demanding, where people learned to rely on one another and find joy even in hardship,” Han said.
“They reflect the beauty of hard work and the open-hearted spirit of people in southern Vietnam. That spirit remains woven into everyday life in the river delta," he said.

title: Gările uitate de pe calea ferată Sibiu - Sighișoara, readuse la viață de voluntari. Proiect inedit de salvare a clădirilor feroviare
content:
Video Gările uitate de pe calea ferată Sibiu - Sighișoara, readuse la viață de voluntari. Proiect inedit de salvare a clădirilor feroviare
Două stații feroviare de pe Valea Hârtibaciului (județul Sibiu), străbătută în trecut de calea ferată îngustă Sibiu – Sighișoara, își schimbă înfățișarea cu ajutorul voluntarilor. Linia veche de peste un secol păstrează numeroase clădiri istorice, dar a fost dezafectată în cea mai mare parte. Un segment al acesteia a fost reactivat ca reper turistic.
O călătorie între Sibiu și Sighișoara, prin Agnita, le oferă turiștilor ocazia de a vedea, înșirate de-a lungul șoselei care străbate mai multe așezări cu origini săsești și biserici fortificate, rămășițele traseului fostei căi ferate care lega, de la începutul secolului XX, cele două orașe transilvane.
În unele locuri, calea ferată îngustă a dispărut de mai multe decenii. În altele, a fost dezafectată după 1990. În ultimii ani însă, Asociația Prietenii Mocăniței și colaboratorii săi au repus în funcțiune șapte kilometri de linie între Cornățel și Hosman, pe care sunt organizate curse turistice în perioada aprilie–octombrie. Asociația lucrează în prezent la refacerea următorilor șase kilometri, până la Cașolț, iar, pe termen mai lung, își propune continuarea traseului de la Hosman spre Nocrich.
„Pe acest segment, traversele au fost scoase de pe terasament. Probabil că s-a încercat furtul lor, fără succes, iar noi trebuie să le reașezăm. Dacă pe traseul spre Hosman vorbim deja despre lucrări periodice de întreținere, între Cornățel și Cașolț este nevoie de defrișări ample. Au crescut copaci și arbuști chiar în mijlocul liniei. Practic, trebuie să desțelenim traseul. În gara Cașolț va trebui să construim și o linie de abatere. În prezent există un singur fir, iar pentru manevrarea locomotivei avem nevoie de încă o linie și de cel puțin două macazuri”, relata recent, pentru Adevărul, Horia Dinu, de la Asociația Prietenii Mocăniței.
În prezent, cei șapte kilometri ai traseului de cale ferată îngustă reactivați de asociație, cu ajutorul voluntarilor, organizațiilor neguvernamentale și localnicilor, atrag aproape 10.000 de turiști anual. Pe restul traseului, alte clădiri și instalații feroviare, unele clasate ca monumente istorice, așteaptă să primească o șansă la revitalizare.
Depozitul vechi din gara Cornățel, refăcut cu voluntari
Două dintre aceste clădiri au primit recent o astfel de șansă, prin intervenții realizate de Asociația Monumentum, prin programul „Ambulanța pentru Monumente”, împreună cu Asociația Prietenii Mocăniței: vechiul depozit de lemn din gara Cornățel și gara din Alțâna.
Calea ferată îngustă de pe Valea Hârtibaciului renaște cu ajutorul voluntarilor. „Avem 9.000–10.000 de turiști anual”La Cornățel, voluntarii și meșterii au început în septembrie 2026 reconstrucția vechiului depozit de mărfuri, ridicat în urmă cu aproximativ 110 ani. Intervenția urmărește refacerea fidelă a clădirii degradate, cu tehnici tradiționale și materiale recuperate.
Asociația Prietenii Mocăniței a arătat că cele două intervenții fac parte dintr-un demers comun de salvare a patrimoniului feroviar al Văii Hârtibaciului.
„În această perioadă, alături de prietenii noștri de la Ambulanța pentru Monumente, lucrăm la două proiecte importante pentru salvarea patrimoniului feroviar de pe Valea Hârtibaciului: refacerea vechiului depozit de lemn din gara Cornățel și a acoperișului gării din Alțâna”, a transmis asociația.
În paralel cu intervenția de la Cornățel, voluntarii au început lucrările și la gara din Alțâna, parte a ansamblului-monument istoric al fostei căi ferate înguste Sibiu–Agnita.
„În paralel cu intervenția de la Cornățel am început lucrările de punere în siguranță a haltei de la Alțâna, care face parte din ansamblul-monument istoric al căii ferate înguste Sibiu–Agnita. Lucrările vizează reparații la structura foarte degradată a acoperișului, la învelitoare, pazie, burlane și jgheaburi”, a transmis Ambulanța pentru Monumente.
Calea ferată care lega Sibiul de Sighișoara
Calea ferată îngustă de pe Valea Hârtibaciului are o istorie de peste un secol. Construcția sa a început în 1895, iar primul tronson, între Sighișoara și Agnita, cu o lungime de circa 48 de kilometri, a fost dat în folosință la sfârșitul secolului al XIX-lea.
Legătura dintre Agnita și Sibiu, lungă de aproximativ 62 de kilometri, a fost finalizată în 1910, când a fost deschisă și ramificația Cornățel–Vurpăr. Întregul sistem ajunsese la aproximativ 123 de kilometri.
Linia era folosită atât pentru transportul călătorilor, cât și al mărfurilor, în special al lemnului. Trenurile circulau lent prin Valea Hârtibaciului, printre sate săsești, biserici fortificate și colinele sudului Transilvaniei.
Declinul a început în anii ’60. Tronsonul Sighișoara–Agnita a fost închis în 1965, iar liniile rămase au supraviețuit încă mai multe decenii. Ruta Cornățel–Vurpăr a fost închisă în 1997, iar în 2001 au încetat și ultimele curse regulate pe traseul Sibiu–Agnita.
În 2007, calea ferată a fost clasată drept monument istoric. Ulterior, voluntarii Asociației Prietenii Mocăniței au început recuperarea unor segmente ale liniei, iar în 2015 au reușit să reactiveze porțiunea Cornățel–Hosman. De atunci, mocănița a revenit treptat în peisajul Văii Hârtibaciului, de această dată ca atracție turistică și proiect de salvare a patrimoniului feroviar.

title: A light of learning glows in Gaza
content:
A light of learning glows in Gaza
Despite the wreckage of war, many more Palestinian children have returned to school in the territory, a testament to their innocence, curiosity, and desire to be skilled for a life of progress.
This week, thousands of excited children in Gaza took part in a ritual seen as normal in much of the world: going back to school. Instead of being in classrooms with whiteboards and desks, however, most sat on the floor in makeshift structures or tents. School supplies were scarce and costly. Teachers were few.
Nearly three years of a war between Hamas and Israel have devastated most school buildings and staff.
Nevertheless, to many in Gaza, the fact that the schools even opened was testament to every child’s desire to be inspired, curious, and skilled for a life of progress. An estimated 540,000 children – the most since the war began – returned to in-person schooling. Working together, Gaza's residents and international aid agencies upheld the ideal of maintaining a decent life for children, in part because they are the most innocent in any war.
“Today was a beautiful day for me,” one mother told Al Jazeera, as she walked her two young sons to the first day of school Sept. 19. “My children ... were excited and they went to bed early,” she said. “I prepared them as if it were a normal school day.”
Children in many war zones, from Ukraine to Sudan, seek joy in learning and friendship in schooling. And a structured educational experience enhances their stability and trust during uncertain times.
In Gaza, a return to prewar life still seems distant and daunting: More than 1 million people have no permanent shelter, and 85% of buildings are damaged or destroyed. In late July, Hamas, the terrorist group that has controlled Gaza for 20 years, said it would begin disarming, dependent on Israel’s phased withdrawal of its troops.
As that peace process drags on, Gaza’s school system struggles to shape a new normal. One essential reform, some observers say, is to reject parts of the official curriculum that glorify violence and ethnically or religiously based hatred.
“For Gaza to have any chance of a different future,” according to Herb Keinon, an analyst with The Jerusalem Post, it needs to “free itself from an educational culture that demonizes Jews ... and presents violence and ‘martyrdom’ as heroic.”
One Palestinian American strongly agrees. Dr. David Hasan, a researcher and professor at Duke University, has set up a network of free schools in Gaza. These “Academies of Hope” – currently serving 21,000 students – provide meals and healthcare to students as well as learning.
More than that, they offer school lessons that do not demonize Jews or glorify “perpetrators of violence against Israel,” The New York Times reported earlier this year. For instance, a math problem counting “martyrs” killed in uprisings is replaced by one that compares the number of fans at soccer matches.

title: Línea 2 promueve la movilidad sostenible entre escolares de Ate y Santa Anita
content:
En el marco de la Semana de la Movilidad Sostenible 2026, la Línea 2 del Metro de Lima y Callao desarrolló una nueva edición del Metro Educa, su programa educativo orientado a promover la Cultura Metro y formar usuarios informados y responsables.


Estudiantes de instituciones educativas de Ate y Santa Anita —como Alfonso Ugarte, San Patricio, Diego Thomson, Dulce Caminito de Jesús, entre otros— recorrieron la Etapa 1ª comprendida entre las estaciones Evitamiento y Mercado Santa Anita. Durante la visita, conocieron de cerca el funcionamiento del primer metro subterráneo del país y reforzaron conceptos clave sobre seguridad, accesibilidad y movilidad sostenible.
La experiencia incluyó el reconocimiento de los niveles de estación, el correcto embarque y desembarque con puertas automáticas de andén, el uso de zonas preferenciales y la gestión adecuada de residuos. Asimismo, la jornada enfatizó las ventajas del transporte eléctrico para el cuidado del ambiente, concluyendo con dinámicas lúdicas de reforzamiento.
Impacto y resultados del programa
La evaluación aplicada al término de la jornada reflejó un alto grado de receptividad por parte de la comunidad escolar:
- 99 % de los participantes consideró útil la información recibida para viajar de manera segura.
- 88 % incrementó su conciencia sobre el impacto ambiental y social del sistema ferroviario.
- 98 % asumió el compromiso de cuidar la infraestructura, respetar la señalización y disponer correctamente los residuos.
Con esta iniciativa, la Línea 2 reafirma su compromiso con la comunidad al generar espacios de aprendizaje que promueven la Cultura Metro, el civismo y el cuidado del bien público, formando a las nuevas generaciones en el uso responsable del transporte y la movilidad sostenible.
